content: Uteroglobin, also referred to as secretoglobin family 1A member 1 (SCGB1A1), is a protein encoded by the SCGB1A1 gene in humans. This protein belongs to the secretoglobin family, which consists of small, secreted, disulfide-bridged dimeric proteins that are exclusively found in mammals. Uteroglobin is a homodimeric protein linked by antiparallel disulfide bonds, and it exhibits multifunctional properties. It is expressed in various tissues and is known by several names, including uteroglobin (UG, UGB), uteroglobin-like antigen (UGL), blastokinin, club-cell secretory protein (CCSP), Clara-cell 16 kD protein (17 kD in rats/mice), club-cell-specific 10 kD protein (CC10), human protein 1, urine protein 1 (UP-1), polychlorinated biphenyl-binding protein (PCB-BP), human club cell phospholipid-binding protein (hCCPBP), and secretoglobin 1A member 1 (SCGB1A1). Notably, this protein is specifically expressed in club cells located in the lungs. The exact physiological role of uteroglobin remains unclear. However, several potential functions have been proposed: 1. Immunomodulation: Uteroglobin may play a role in modulating immune responses. 2. Progesterone Binding: It exhibits weak progesterone-binding activity in some animals, with particularly weak binding observed in humans. Interestingly, uteroglobin itself is a progesterone-induced gene in the endometrium of lagomorphs. 3. Inhibition of Phospholipase A2: In vitro studies suggest that uteroglobin can inhibit the activity of phospholipase A2. 4. Binding to Phospholipids: Uteroglobin has been shown to bind phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylinositol. 5. Interaction with Fibronectin: Uteroglobin binds to fibronectin, and its absence in knockout mice of the inbred C57Bl6 strain leads to the development of a glomerulopathy resembling Goodpasture's syndrome. This condition is thought to result from fibronectin binding of IgA, which might be preventable through uteroglobin replacement therapy. However, contrary to findings in animal models, human genetic data suggest that the observed effects may be indirect. Knockout mice of the inbred 129 strain, which lack uteroglobin, appear to have a healthy phenotype without developing glomerulopathy. However, these mice exhibit physiological differences in their responses to respiratory challenges. Specific phenotypic changes observed in these mice include: Reduced bioaccumulation of biphenyls. Increased susceptibility to hyperoxic challenges, accompanied by elevated levels of interleukin-13 (IL-13) and interleukin-6 (IL-6). Alterations in the morphology of club cells. These findings highlight the complex and context-dependent roles of uteroglobin in physiological and pathological processes.
